# Block 1: Reproducibility {.unnumbered} > **Materials:** Download all files from the course OSF page: **** :::{.callout-note} **Before we start:** Download `celegans_repro_raw.csv` and `celegans_repro_final.csv` from and place them in your working directory. We will load them throughout the session. **Also install READMEBuilder**, which you'll use in Part 4: `install.packages("pak")`, then `pak::pak("EIvimeyCook/READMEBuilder@development")`. ::: --- ## Part 1: What is reproducibility? {#repro-what} *⏱ ~20 minutes* :::{.callout-tip} **Opening activity: why don't *you* share?** *(post your answer in Slack)* Think about your most recent or current project. 1. Is the **data** publicly available? Is the **code**? 2. If either is not — why not? Be honest. Too busy? Worried someone will find an error? Not sure how or where? Worried about being scooped? Code too messy to show anyone? Write down your real reasons. [Gomes et al. (2022)](https://doi.org/10.1098/rspb.2022.1113) surveyed researchers and grouped the barriers people actually report: knowledge gaps, fear of scrutiny, time cost, misaligned career incentives. Keep your list; at the end of the session we will compare it with theirs. > **Gomes, D.G.E., et al. (2022).** Why don't we share data and code? Perceived barriers and benefits to public archiving practices. *Proceedings of the Royal Society B*, 289, 20221113. ::: ### Analytical and computational reproducibility "Reproducibility" means different things to different people, and the fixes differ too. [Goodman et al. (2016)](https://doi.org/10.1126/scitranslmed.aaf5027) argue for keeping the meanings apart. We use three: **Analytical reproducibility:** given the same raw data, would a different analyst following the same stated methods reach the same conclusions? Methods sections leave dozens of choices unstated (exclusions, missing values, transformations, random effects). These "researcher degrees of freedom" ([Simmons et al. 2011](https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797611417632)) let honest analysts end up in different places. **Computational reproducibility:** given the same data *and* code, do you get identical outputs? It's the lower bar, and most of the papers that have been checked still fail it. **Replicability:** does the finding hold with new data? :::{.callout-note} **Shorthand:** Computational reproducibility asks "did you do what your code says?" Analytical reproducibility asks "would a reasonable analyst agree with your approach?" Replicability asks "does it still hold with new data?" ::: ### The replication crisis starts with reproducibility Across psychology, biomedicine, ecology and evolutionary biology, large-scale efforts to repeat published studies have found that a substantial share of findings do not hold up. This is the **replication crisis** (also called the reproducibility crisis; the two terms are used more or less interchangeably). It is tempting to treat this purely as a problem of *replicability*, of effects that were never real. But a finding cannot even be evaluated unless its analysis is reproducible in the first place. If the data and code are not available, or are available but do not run, nobody can check whether the published result actually follows from the data. A non-reproducible literature is one where genuine errors stay hidden, and where a failed replication cannot be diagnosed: was the original analysis wrong, or is the effect simply fragile? **Lack of reproducibility is both a problem in its own right and an upstream cause of the wider crisis**: it removes the evidence trail we need to tell sound science from artefact. So how often does that first step work? :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} **Exercise: estimate the funnel (3 minutes)** :::: ::::{.task-container} [Kellner et al. (2025)](https://doi.org/10.1002/ecy.4475) checked the archived data and code of 497 ecology papers that modelled species distribution and abundance. Write down your estimate for each stage, then post them in Slack (for example `60, 40, 20`) **before** you check them in the boxes. Which stage were you furthest out on, and why do you think that is? 1. What % of the papers archived their data? 2. What % archived their code? 3. What % had code that ran without errors? :::: :::
How close were you to 7%? Here's the pipeline across recent surveys: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Reproducibility rates at four sequential stages of the analysis pipeline. Percentages are of all sampled papers unless noted; Trisovic et al. (2022) is a percentage of archived R files.
Study (sample) % of papers
Data archived
Cooper et al. (2026) — 1,861 BES papers (2017–24) 90%
Kambouris et al. (2024) — 177 EcoEvo meta-analyses (2015–17) 75%
Kellner et al. (2025) — 497 papers, 9 ecology journals (2018–22) 50%
Code archived
Kellner et al. (2025) 33%
Cooper et al. (2026) 31%
Culina et al. (2020) — ecology 27%
Kambouris et al. (2024) 16%

````` ::: :::
- **Code often isn't archived.** In the British Ecological Society journals, 97% of papers that used data archived it, but only 35% of those that used code archived the code ([Cooper et al. 2026](https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210x.70338)). - **Archived code often doesn't run.** 74% of more than 9,000 archived R files failed on the first attempt ([Trisovic et al. 2022](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41597-022-01143-6)). - **Documentation is thin.** About a third of the BES papers had no README. The funnel is getting wider at the top, but it's still very narrow at the bottom. :::{.callout-note collapse="true"} ## The details: what each study found **First, the code is often simply not archived.** [Cooper et al. (2026)](https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210x.70338), surveying 1,861 papers published 2017–2024 across the seven British Ecological Society journals, found that data archiving has become near-universal: 97% of papers that used data archived it, although that figure is held up by mandatory journal policies rather than community norms. Code is a different story: **only 35% of papers that used code also archived it** (about 31% of all sampled papers). The picture is similar or worse in samples without strong code-sharing mandates: [Kellner et al. (2025)](https://doi.org/10.1002/ecy.4475), across nine ecology journals, found data *and* code available for only 28% of 497 papers; [Kambouris et al. (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0300333) found data and code shared for only 15% of 177 ecology and evolutionary biology meta-analyses published 2015–17. **Second, even when code is archived, it frequently does not run.** Kellner et al. (2025) attempted to execute the R code accompanying those 497 papers and found that **only 7% of all papers (and only 27% of the papers whose archived data and code could be tested) ran without error**. The most common causes were missing or misnamed files, missing R objects, and reliance on deprecated R packages (17 papers, most of them broken by the retirement of spatial packages such as `rgdal` and `maptools`). [Trisovic et al. (2022)](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41597-022-01143-6), executing more than 9,000 archived R files from the Harvard Dataverse, found 74% failed on the first attempt and 56% still failed after automated cleaning. Kambouris et al. (2024) successfully reproduced the target result from 27–73% of the 26 ecology and evolution meta-analyses that shared both data and code, the range depending on how strictly "successful reproduction" was defined. **Documentation quality is the other half of the problem.** Cooper et al. (2026) also recorded that around a third of papers had no README to explain their archived files, and that the quality of the READMEs that did exist varied substantially. Sharing rates have crept up over the last decade, from ~27% in [Culina et al. (2020)](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pbio.3000763) to ~31–35% in Cooper et al. (2026), but there is no sign that the execution rate has improved: only 7% of papers in Kellner et al. (2025) had code that ran. The funnel may be getting wider at the top, but it is still very narrow at the bottom. Sharing is necessary but not sufficient; archived data and code also have to be *good enough to run and reproduce the result*. ::: ### Quick check :::::{.quiz} ::::{.quiz-q} A colleague downloads your archived data and your archived script, runs it, and gets different numbers from the paper. Which kind of reproducibility has failed? :::{.quiz-explain} **Computational reproducibility**: the same data and the same code should give the same outputs. Analytical reproducibility asks whether a *different* analyst, following the same stated methods, would reach the same conclusions; replicability needs new data. ::: :::: ::::{.quiz-q} Kellner et al. (2025) tried to run the R code from 497 papers that modelled species distribution and abundance. What share of *all* the papers had code that ran without error?
:::{.quiz-explain} **About 7%.** The 27% is a trap: it is the share of the papers whose data and code could actually be tested. Most papers fell out before that point, because their code was never archived. ::: :::: ::::{.quiz-q} True or false? Data archiving in the British Ecological Society journals is now close to universal, so the reproducibility problem in ecology is largely solved. :::{.quiz-explain} **False.** Cooper et al. (2026) found near-universal *data* archiving, but only 35% of papers that used code archived it, and Kellner et al. (2025) found that only 7% of papers had code that ran. ::: :::: ::::: ### Questionable research practices Not every failure to replicate is an honest accident. **Questionable research practices** (QRPs) are choices that make a result look stronger than the data support, usually without anyone setting out to mislead. [Fraser et al. (2018)](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0200303) surveyed 807 ecologists and evolutionary biologists and asked whether they had ever done each of these, at least once: - **Cherry-picking:** not reporting results because they were not statistically significant: **64%**. (Reporting them in a results table or the supplement is fine; leaving them out altogether is the problem.) - **p-hacking:** collecting more data after checking whether the results were significant: **42%**. - **HARKing** (*hypothesising after the results are known*): reporting an unexpected finding as though it had been predicted from the start: **51%**. These rates are comparable to those reported for psychologists. Each practice exploits the "garden of forking paths" you'll meet in Part 2: with enough defensible choices, some route through the analysis will often give p < 0.05. You'll see how easily this happens at the end of Part 2. Shared, readable code does not prevent QRPs, but it makes them visible; preregistration and registered reports go further by fixing the analysis before the data are seen. ### Spot the QRP :::::{.quiz} ::::{.quiz-q} Spot the QRP: *"We also measured lifespan, but as it showed no difference between strains it is not reported here."* :::{.quiz-explain} **Cherry-picking.** A result is left out *because* it was not significant, so readers never learn it was tested. Fraser et al. (2018) found that 64% of ecologists and evolutionary biologists had done this at least once. ::: :::: ::::{.quiz-q} Spot the QRP: *"Lifespan did not differ between strains (Table S3)."* :::{.quiz-explain} **This is fine.** The non-significant result is reported, here in a supplementary table, so nothing is hidden. Reporting null results is exactly what avoids cherry-picking. ::: :::: ::::{.quiz-q} Spot the QRP: *"We added worms in batches until the difference between strains reached significance (p = 0.048)."* :::{.quiz-explain} **p-hacking.** Collecting more data after checking the p-value, and stopping when it falls below 0.05, raises the false-positive rate well above 5%. 42% of the researchers Fraser et al. surveyed had done it. ::: :::: ::::{.quiz-q} Spot the QRP: your plan predicted an effect of daf-2 on both diets. You found one under fasting only, and the paper's introduction now says *"we predicted the effect would appear under dietary restriction"*. :::{.quiz-explain} **HARKing**: hypothesising after the results are known. The prediction was rewritten to match the result, which makes a chance finding look like a confirmed hypothesis. 51% of the researchers Fraser et al. surveyed had done it. ::: :::: ::::: --- ## Part 2: Many analysts, many answers {#repro-multiverse} *⏱ ~48 minutes* ### Background: the garden of forking paths Even honest analysts with the same data and question can reach different answers: [Gelman & Loken (2013)](http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/unpublished/forking.pdf) call it the "garden of forking paths". It isn't p-hacking; each choice just looks inevitable in hindsight. **Many-analysts** studies test this directly ([Silberzahn et al. 2018](https://doi.org/10.1177/2515245917747646); [Gould et al. 2025](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12915-024-02101-x)). Gould et al. gave 174 teams the same ecology datasets, and their estimates spread widely. Reviewers' ratings of each analysis didn't predict which teams landed near the average. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The many-analysts project (Gould et al. 2025).](images/many_analysts.png){fig-align='center' width=80%} ::: ::: ### You are the analyst Now you experience this directly. You are given the *C. elegans* reproduction dataset from the course OSF page and a deliberately vague question. Analyse it however seems most reasonable to you. **The biology:** *C. elegans* is a workhorse model organism in genetics and ageing research. The dataset records each worm's **total offspring** — its lifetime reproductive output — from an experiment crossing two interventions: | Variable | Meaning | |---|---| | `worm_id` | Individual worm identifier | | `B` | Batch (1–6) — worms run in separate cohorts | | `strain` | `daf` = daf-2 RNAi (knocks down insulin/IGF-1 signalling; extends lifespan and alters reproduction); `empty_vector` = control RNAi | | `diet` | `AL` = ad libitum (fed freely); `EODF` = every-other-day fasting (dietary restriction) | | `TO` | Total offspring — lifetime count of live progeny per worm | **The question:** *Does daf-2 RNAi affect reproduction?* That is all you are told. Now analyse it. :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} **Exercise: analyse the worm data (20 minutes)** :::: ::::{.task-container} Load `celegans_repro_final.csv` from and answer: **does daf-2 RNAi affect total offspring?** You must decide: - What to do with any unusual values in the data - Whether to include diet as a covariate or factor - Whether batch (`B`) should be a fixed or random effect, or ignored - What statistical model to use (t-test? linear model? mixed model? a count model such as a Poisson or negative-binomial GLMM?) - Whether to use `TO` as-is or transform it **Before running anything**, write down your three most important analytical decisions and why. Then run your analysis. :::{.callout-note collapse="true"} ## New to models? A worked example on different data This example uses `grouseticks`, which comes with `lme4`: ticks counted on red grouse chicks, at different altitudes and locations, in different years. It has the same shape as the worm data: a **count** outcome (`TICKS`, like `TO`), a **two-level factor** you want to compare (`YEAR`, like `strain`), a **covariate** (`cHEIGHT`, altitude, like `diet`) and a **grouping factor** (`LOCATION`, like batch `B`). The question: did chicks carry more ticks in 1996 than in 1995? ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) library(lme4) library(emmeans) ticks <- grouseticks |> filter(YEAR %in% c("95", "96")) |> mutate(YEAR = droplevels(YEAR)) # 1. Compare two group means (a t-test, written as a linear model) m1 <- lm(TICKS ~ YEAR, data = ticks) # 2. Add a covariate that also affects the outcome m2 <- lm(TICKS ~ YEAR + cHEIGHT, data = ticks) # 3. Chicks from the same location are not independent: # give LOCATION a random intercept (a mixed model) m3 <- lmer(TICKS ~ YEAR + cHEIGHT + (1 | LOCATION), data = ticks) # 4. TICKS is a count (0, 1, 2, ...), so use a count model: # a negative-binomial GLMM (or family = poisson with glmer()) m4 <- glmer.nb(TICKS ~ YEAR + cHEIGHT + (1 | LOCATION), data = ticks) # 5. Answer the question on the same scale for each model: # the difference in ticks per chick, 1996 minus 1995 emmeans(m4, ~ YEAR) |> regrid() |> contrast("trt.vs.ctrl", ref = 1, adjust = "none") |> # ref = 1: the first level, 1995 confint() # 6. Check a model before you trust it plot(m3) # residuals against fitted values: look for funnels or curves ``` ::: How to choose, in four questions: 1. **What kind of outcome is it?** A continuous measurement suits `lm()`/`lmer()`; a count suits a Poisson or negative-binomial model. 2. **What else affects it?** Add it as a covariate (`+ cHEIGHT`). 3. **Are some observations grouped?** Worms from the same batch, or chicks from the same location, are more alike than random ones: add a random intercept, `(1 | group)`. 4. **Does the model fit?** Look at the residuals. Run step 5 on each of `m1` to `m4` and the 1996 − 1995 difference comes out as about 5.2, 3.3, 5.7 and 3.2 ticks, and one of the four intervals includes zero. Same data, same question, different defensible answers: exactly what you are about to find with the worms. ::: :::{.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Report your result with this code ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # install.packages("emmeans") library(emmeans) # Works for lm, lmer, glmer, glmer.nb. regrid() back-transforms to the # response scale BEFORE the contrast. For identity-link models (lm/lmer) # it changes nothing; for log-link models (glmer/glmer.nb) it turns the # default rate ratio into a difference in offspring. # "trt.vs.ctrl" with ref = "empty_vector" always gives daf - empty_vector, # whatever order the strain levels are in. emmeans(model, ~ strain) |> regrid() |> contrast("trt.vs.ctrl", ref = "empty_vector", adjust = "none") |> confint() # -> "daf - empty_vector" estimate 95% CI in offspring per worm # (negative = daf worms had fewer offspring) # If the estimate says "nonEst", one strain x diet group is empty: # check count(your_data, strain, diet) for a stray label. # glmer() and glmer.nb() stop with an error if any TO is negative: # decide what to do about that value first. # A log written in the formula, e.g. lm(log(TO) ~ strain), is detected # automatically, so the template above works as it is. Only if you logged # the variable in a separate step, e.g. dat$logTO <- log(dat$TO) and then # lm(logTO ~ strain), do you need to tell emmeans about the transformation: emmeans(model, ~ strain) |> update(tran = "log") |> regrid() |> contrast("trt.vs.ctrl", ref = "empty_vector", adjust = "none") |> confint() ``` ::: Report the **estimate, the 95% confidence interval, and the units** (offspring per worm). If you prefer a multiplicative effect, report a ratio as well, but at minimum everyone reports `daf - empty_vector` on the response scale so that we are all comparing like with like. ::: :::{.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Why this code? Different analysts will pick different models, e.g. a Gaussian linear (or mixed) model, a Poisson GLMM, a negative-binomial GLMM, or a log-transformed linear model. Each one reports the `daf` effect on a different scale: - A linear model on `TO` returns an **additive difference** — "daf reduces offspring by X per worm." - A Poisson or NB GLMM with a log link returns a **log-scale coefficient**, which back-transforms to a **rate ratio** — "daf has 0.7× the offspring of controls." - A linear model on `log(TO)` returns a log-scale difference, which back-transforms to a ratio. These numbers are not directly comparable between participants. **`emmeans`** puts them all on the response scale (offspring per worm) in two steps: compute the estimated marginal means, then take the contrast between `daf` and `empty_vector`. We also need everyone to report the difference **the same way round**. The default `"pairwise"` contrast subtracts in factor-level order, so with `empty_vector` as the first (reference) level, as the cleaning script later sets it, you get `empty_vector - daf` and a drop in offspring shows up as a positive number. Leave the levels in alphabetical order instead and you get `daf - empty_vector`. Everyone therefore reports **`daf - empty_vector`**: a negative estimate means daf worms had fewer offspring. The template above fixes this by naming `empty_vector` as the control, which works whatever order your factor levels are in. For log-link models we use `regrid()` first, which back-transforms the means to the response scale **before** the contrast, so the result is a *difference* in offspring, not the default rate ratio. ::: **Post one line in Slack:** `estimate, lower, upper, batch`, for example `-48, -70, -26, yes`. That's your daf − empty_vector estimate (negative means daf worms had fewer offspring), its 95% CI, and whether you modelled batch as a random effect. Then post your three key decisions. :::: ::: ### The results **Before you look at the plot**, write down how many of the group you expect to have found a significant effect of daf-2, then compare. We'll collect your estimates and draw the class plot live. Until a course's estimates are added, the book shows 16 analyses we ran ourselves on the same file, each with different but defensible choices. Points left of the dashed line mean daf worms had fewer offspring than controls. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Results from the many-analysts activity. Each point is one participant's estimate of the daf-2 RNAi effect on C. elegans total offspring (daf minus empty_vector, offspring per worm). Negative values mean daf worms had fewer offspring.](06-reproducibility_files/figure-html/many-analysts-demo-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: :::{.callout-note} **Debrief (5 minutes):** 1. How much did the estimates vary? Did anyone get a non-significant result while others got significant? 2. Who modelled batch as a random effect? Did that change the conclusion? 3. Who used a count model (Poisson / negative-binomial) vs a plain linear model? Does the model choice matter here? 4. What would the published literature look like if each of you submitted your analysis independently? ::: ### Why this matters That spread comes from underspecified methods, not noise. The fix is **transparency**: record every decision so a reader can judge it. That's where TADA! ([Ivimey-Cook et al. 2025](https://doi.org/10.32942/X2D93K)) and the SORTEE guidelines ([Pick et al. 2026](https://doi.org/10.24072/pcjournal.687)) come in, and it's what code review (this afternoon) is designed to catch. ### Wrap-up: run it until it works :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} **Exercise: run it until it works (3 minutes)** :::: ::::{.task-container} The function below repeats one experiment over and over: 30 worms of each strain, with offspring counts drawn from **the same distribution**, so strain has no real effect. On each trial it also tries four common analyses on the same data: a t-test, a t-test on log counts, a t-test with "outliers" removed, and a Wilcoxon test. It stops at the first trial where any of them gives p < 0.05, and tells you the trial and the analysis that "worked". Run the block once and post both in Slack. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} run_until_significant <- function() { trial <- 0 repeat { trial <- trial + 1 # one experiment: 30 worms per strain, all drawn from the SAME distribution worms <- data.frame(strain = rep(c("empty_vector", "daf"), each = 30), TO = rnbinom(60, mu = 250, size = 12)) # four analyses you might try on the same data keep <- abs(worms$TO - mean(worms$TO)) < 2 * sd(worms$TO) p <- c("t-test" = t.test(TO ~ strain, data = worms)$p.value, "log counts" = t.test(log(TO + 1) ~ strain, data = worms)$p.value, "outliers removed" = t.test(TO ~ strain, data = worms[keep, ])$p.value, "Wilcoxon test" = wilcox.test(TO ~ strain, data = worms, exact = FALSE)$p.value) cat(sprintf("Trial %d: %s\n", trial, paste(sprintf("%s p = %.3f", names(p), p), collapse = ", "))) if (any(p < 0.05)) break } best <- names(which.min(p)) cat(sprintf("\nSignificant on trial %d (%s, p = %.3f).\nPost in Slack: %d, %s\n", trial, best, min(p), trial, best)) invisible(list(trial = trial, analysis = best)) } run_until_significant() ``` ::: :::: :::
There is no real difference between the strains in any trial: both are drawn from the same distribution. The "effect" you found is chance alone, two random samples that happened to land far apart. One honest test has a 5% chance of such a false positive. Trying four analyses on the same data raises that to about 8% per trial, so the "discoveries" come sooner: in our simulations, half of people got one by trial 9 (it would be trial 14 with a single test), and the occasional unlucky person needed over 100. Look at Slack: which analysis "worked" most often? "Outliers removed" won most often in our runs, because deciding what counts as an outlier is the most flexible choice of the four. The chance result isn't the problem: every honest test carries a 5% risk. Hiding the trials that failed, and the analyses that didn't work, is. Now imagine a lab that repeats the experiment until it "works" and writes up only that trial: cherry-picking at the level of whole experiments, with the failures left in the file drawer. Trying analysis after analysis on one dataset and reporting only the one that worked is p-hacking: the forking paths you have just seen in the many-analysts plot, walked on purpose. Do both, and a published "p = 0.04" can come from the ninth experiment and the third analysis, with nothing in the paper to say so. A p-value means what it says only if it was the only test you ran, or if you report every test you ran. That is why the rest of today is about making every step visible: the data, the decisions and the code.
### Quick check :::::{.quiz} ::::{.quiz-q} Gelman & Loken's "garden of forking paths" describes:
:::{.quiz-explain} No deliberate p-hacking is needed. Honest analysts make one reasonable choice after another, and the route they took looks like the only one in hindsight, even though many others were just as defensible. ::: :::: ::::{.quiz-q} True or false? In Gould et al. (2025), analyses that peer reviewers rated highly produced estimates closer to the average. :::{.quiz-explain} **False.** Reviewers' ratings did not predict how far a team's estimate lay from the average: well-rated analyses were as spread out as poorly rated ones. ::: :::: ::::{.quiz-q} Your `"pairwise"` contrast prints `empty_vector - daf = 45`. What number should you post in Slack? :::{.quiz-explain} **−45.** Everyone reports `daf - empty_vector`, so flip the sign. A positive `empty_vector - daf` of 45 means daf worms had 45 *fewer* offspring. ::: :::: ::::{.quiz-q} You fit a negative-binomial GLMM (log link) and run `emmeans(model, ~ strain) |> contrast("trt.vs.ctrl", ref = "empty_vector")`, forgetting `regrid()`. What does the contrast compare?
:::{.quiz-explain} Without `regrid()` the contrast is worked out on the log scale. A difference of logs back-transforms to a *ratio* ("daf worms have 0.7× the offspring"), not a difference ("45 fewer"). `regrid()` moves to the response scale first. ::: :::: ::::: --- ## Part 3: Diagnosing a bad dataset and script {#repro-diagnosis} *⏱ ~30 minutes* Now we look systematically at the raw data file. `celegans_repro_raw.csv` contains the same experiment but before any cleaning. Every problem in it is a real type of problem that appears in published archives. ### Data quality audit ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) # Load the raw data — download from https://osf.io/jgeq9/ dat_raw <- read_csv("celegans_repro_raw.csv", trim_ws = FALSE) # keep spaces exactly as typed, so none are hidden # First look dim(dat_raw) glimpse(dat_raw) summary(dat_raw) ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # Check each variable for problems # strain values dat_raw |> count(strain) # Diet values dat_raw |> count(diet) # TO (total offspring) range dat_raw |> summarise(min = min(TO, na.rm = TRUE), max = max(TO, na.rm = TRUE), n_na = sum(is.na(TO))) # worm_id problems dat_raw |> filter(is.na(worm_id)) # Duplicate rows? dat_raw |> filter(!is.na(worm_id)) |> group_by(worm_id, B) |> filter(n() > 1) |> arrange(worm_id) # Rows where everything is NA except TO dat_raw |> filter(is.na(strain)) ``` ::: :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} **Exercise: data audit (10 minutes)** :::: ::::{.task-container} The raw file contains **nine** data quality problems. Run the code above and, for each problem you find, write one line: **the problem, the column, and what it would do to an analysis** (for example: *`TO` has −46; offspring can't be negative; it drags the daf/EODF mean down*). Post your list in Slack, then check it against the solution. Hints: capitalisation, spaces, impossible values, codes pretending to be numbers, rows that shouldn't be there. :::: :::

Partial cleaning like this is common in real archives. ::: :::: ::::: --- ## Part 4: Fixing it with structure, cleaning and a README {#repro-fix} *⏱ ~50 minutes* ### Step 1: Set up the project structure Most analysis projects do not start tidy. Here is a very typical folder structure for this *C. elegans* experiment, with everything dumped in a single directory: ``` REPROCODE_ANALYSIS/ ├── celegans_repro_raw.csv # raw data ├── celegans_repro_final.csv # a "cleaned" copy — but cleaned how? ├── ANALYSIS.R # the analysis script ├── old_code.R # an earlier version, still sitting here ├── celegans_analysis.Rmd # a write-up ├── celegans_analysis.html # the rendered write-up ├── final.jpeg ├── finalplot.jpeg # "finalplot" — so which figure is current? ├── ExtractedFigure1.png ├── Flowchart.jpg └── 4Rs.jpg ``` :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} **Exercise: diagnose the folder (3 minutes)** :::: ::::{.task-container} List every problem you can see in this folder, and for each one, say what you would change (move, rename, delete or add). Post your list in Slack, then compare it with ours. :::: :::
- **Raw and processed data sit side by side.** Which file is safe to overwrite, and how was `celegans_repro_final.csv` made? - **`old_code.R` is dead code**, waiting for a collaborator to run it by mistake. - **Five loose images**: outputs mixed in with the source, with `final` and `finalplot` doing the job of version control. - **No README**: nothing says what to run, or in what order.
This is a normal project; most look like this. (We review `ANALYSIS.R` itself this afternoon; for now we fix the *structure*.) Aim instead for a few standard folders that separate inputs, code and outputs: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) library(here) # Create a proper folder structure dirs <- c("data/raw", "data/processed", "analysis", "figures", "results") for (d in dirs) { dir.create(d, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE) } # Copy the raw data file into data/raw/ — never modify this copy file.copy("celegans_repro_raw.csv", here("data", "raw", "celegans_repro_raw.csv")) cat("Project structure:\n") list.files(recursive = TRUE, include.dirs = TRUE) ``` ::: ### Step 2: A documented cleaning script ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # analysis/01_data_cleaning.R # Author: [your name] # Date: [today] # Purpose: Clean raw C. elegans reproduction data for daf-2 × diet experiment # # Study: Effect of daf-2 RNAi and dietary restriction on total offspring # Organism: Caenorhabditis elegans (N2 background) # Design: 2 strains (daf-2 RNAi vs empty_vector control) × # 2 diets (AL = ad libitum; EODF = every-other-day fasting) # 6 batches (B); multiple worms per batch # # Variables: # worm_id — individual worm ID (integer) # B — batch number (1–6); should be treated as random effect # strain — "daf" = daf-2 RNAi; "empty_vector" = control # diet — "AL" = ad libitum; "EODF" = every-other-day fasting # TO — total offspring (count); 9999 = undocumented code for "not recorded" # # Input: data/raw/celegans_repro_raw.csv # Output: data/processed/celegans_clean.csv # results/exclusion_log.csv library(tidyverse) library(here) # ── 1. Load ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── dat_raw <- read_csv(here("data", "raw", "celegans_repro_raw.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) cat("Raw data:", nrow(dat_raw), "rows\n") # ── 2. Standardise factor levels (case and whitespace) ──────────────────────── # strain: "DAF" is a capitalisation error — same as "daf" # "empty_vector " has trailing whitespace — same as "empty_vector" # diet: "eodf" is a capitalisation error — same as "EODF" dat_std <- dat_raw |> mutate( strain = str_trim(str_to_lower(strain)), diet = str_trim(str_to_upper(diet)) ) cat("After standardisation — strain values:\n") print(count(dat_std, strain)) cat("After standardisation — diet values:\n") print(count(dat_std, diet)) # ── 3. Count structural junk rows ──────────────────────────────────────────── # worm_ids 501–506: strain and diet both NA — data entry artefacts # (count with the same rule we use to remove them in step 4) n_junk <- sum(is.na(dat_std$strain) & is.na(dat_std$diet)) cat("Junk rows (no strain or diet):", n_junk, "\n") # ── 4. Remove junk and duplicate rows ──────────────────────────────────────── dat_std <- dat_std |> filter(!(is.na(strain) & is.na(diet))) # Batch 2 rows appear duplicated — retain first occurrence only. # Rows with a missing worm_id are never treated as duplicates: R would count # two unidentified worms as the "same" worm and silently drop one. n_before_dedup <- nrow(dat_std) dat_std <- dat_std |> filter(is.na(worm_id) | !duplicated(pick(worm_id, B, strain, diet))) n_removed_dupes <- n_before_dedup - nrow(dat_std) cat("Duplicate rows removed:", n_removed_dupes, "\n") # ── 5. Data-quality exclusions and flags ───────────────────────────────────── # Exclusion 1: TO = 9999 — undocumented sentinel meaning "offspring not # recorded". These are missing values, not real counts of zero; we exclude # them and record the count so the loss is visible in the methods section. n_missing <- sum(dat_std$TO == 9999, na.rm = TRUE) cat("Missing offspring (TO = 9999):", n_missing, "excluded\n") # Exclusion 2: TO < 0 — biologically impossible (offspring cannot be negative) # worm_id 112, B=5, daf, EODF: TO = -46 — likely data entry error n_neg <- sum(dat_std$TO < 0, na.rm = TRUE) cat("Negative TO values:", n_neg, "\n") # Flag 1: TO > 1000 and < 9999 — implausible (C. elegans brood size is # typically ~250–350; values in the thousands are not credible) # worm_id 47, B=4, daf, AL: TO = 2850 — likely a typo for 285 # Flag, don't remove: the row stays in the data, marked flag_implausible, # until the value is checked against the original data sheet n_implausible <- sum(dat_std$TO > 1000 & dat_std$TO < 9999, na.rm = TRUE) cat("Implausible TO values (>1000, <9999):", n_implausible, "— flagged, kept pending verification\n") dat_clean <- dat_std |> filter( TO != 9999, # Exclusion 1: missing (9999 sentinel) TO >= 0 # Exclusion 2: impossible ) |> mutate( # Flag 1: kept, but marked so the analysis can leave it out visibly flag_implausible = TO > 1000, # Explicit factor with reference levels strain = factor(strain, levels = c("empty_vector", "daf")), diet = factor(diet, levels = c("AL", "EODF")), B = factor(B) # batch as factor for random effect ) cat("\nFinal clean dataset:", nrow(dat_clean), "worms\n") # ── 6. Save ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── write_csv(dat_clean, here("data", "processed", "celegans_clean.csv")) exclusion_log <- tribble( ~Criterion, ~N, ~Action, "Junk rows (no strain or diet)", n_junk, "Excluded", "Duplicate rows removed", n_removed_dupes, "Excluded", "Missing offspring (TO = 9999)", n_missing, "Excluded", "Impossible count (TO < 0)", n_neg, "Excluded", "Implausible count (TO > 1000, not 9999)", n_implausible, "Flagged, kept" ) write_csv(exclusion_log, here("results", "exclusion_log.csv")) print(exclusion_log) ``` ::: :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} **Exercise: run and inspect the cleaning script (8 minutes)** :::: ::::{.task-container} Copy this script into `analysis/01_data_cleaning.R` in your project and run it. Then answer in Slack: 1. How many worms are in the final clean dataset? 2. Looking at the exclusion log: which exclusion removes the most observations? 3. The script keeps TO = 2850 but marks it in a `flag_implausible` column, rather than deleting it or keeping it unmarked. Why is that the right choice for reproducibility? Where does the decision to leave it out of the analysis now live? 4. Read through the cleaning script, do you understand what it is doing? :::: ::: ### TADA!: the framework behind a reviewable script The cleaning script you just ran is short, but several of its choices were deliberate: the header block, the `here()` calls, the explicit exclusion log and the section dividers. These map onto a small set of principles for analytical code sharing that we use throughout the rest of this course. **TADA!** (*Transferable, Available, Documented, Annotated*) is the minimum an author needs to do to share working analysis code with a paper: | | Principle | In one line | In practice | |---|---|---|---| | **T** | Transferable | Anyone can open and run it, unaltered | Plain `.R` files; relative paths (RStudio project + `here()`); one project folder archived whole; a colleague test-runs it | | **A** | Available | Archived publicly, with a DOI cited in the paper | Zenodo or Figshare (linked to GitHub releases), or Software Heritage; cite the DOI of the version used. GitHub alone, "on request" or Dropbox don't count | | **D** | Documented | A README says how to reuse it | Authors and contact; R and package versions; where the data are; what each file does, run order and run time; a licence | | **A** | Annotated | Comments say what and why | A header per script; per-chunk comments saying what, why, and which result in the paper; section markers | TADA! maps onto the FAIR principles and is how authors meet Stage 3 of the SORTEE guidelines. `renv` and containers help further, but go beyond its minimum. :::{.callout-note collapse="true"} ## The details: each principle in full Ivimey-Cook et al. (2025) propose **TADA!** (*Transferable, Available, Documented, Annotated*): the minimum an author needs to do to share functional analysis code with a paper. The guidelines are built with the FAIR principles in mind, and each letter maps onto one or more of them: Transferable onto *Interoperable*, Available onto *Findable* and *Accessible*, and Documented and Annotated onto *Reusable*. Following TADA! is also how an author meets **Stage 3** of the SORTEE data-editor guidelines (Pick et al. 2026), which we come back to in Part 5. The four letters: - **T: Transferable.** Anyone can open, view and run the code without converting or altering it. - Save code as a plain code file (`.R`, `.py`), never inside a Word document or PDF: copying code out of those changes characters and breaks it. - Use relative file paths, never absolute ones or `setwd()`. An RStudio project together with `here()` is the recommended way. - Keep data and code in one project folder with sub-folders (e.g. `data/raw/`, `data/processed/`, `code/`, `figures/`), and archive that whole folder so the paths still work. - Before archiving, ask a colleague to run the code on their machine. Dependency managers such as `renv`, workflow managers and containers help reproducibility further, but the paper treats them as beyond TADA!'s minimum. - **A: Available.** The code is publicly archived with a persistent identifier, such as a DOI, that is cited in the paper. - Use **Zenodo** or **Figshare**. Both can connect to a GitHub repository and archive each release automatically, with a DOI for every version. **Software Heritage** is another option. - GitHub (and GitLab, Bitbucket and similar) is for *developing* code, not archiving it: it gives no DOI, and files can be changed or deleted after publication. - Cite the DOI of the *version* of the code that produced the paper's results. "Available on request" and a personal Dropbox link do not count: the first decays with careers, the second with subscriptions. - **D: Documented.** A README tells a reader what they need to reuse the code: - the authors, with contact details (these can be anonymised for double-blind review), and the title, abstract and funders of the paper; - the software and its version (e.g. R 4.5.2), and **every package with its version number**, for example as a saved `sessionInfo()` file; - where the data are, ideally with their DOI; - what each file contains, the order to run them, what data they need, what they produce, and how long they take to run; - a **licence** saying how others may use the code: typically **MIT** (permissive) or **GPL** (derivatives must use the same licence). [choosealicense.com](https://choosealicense.com/) helps you pick one. We'll build a README in the next section using READMEBuilder, which the TADA! paper recommends. - **A: Annotated.** Comments inside the code explain what it does and why. - Start each script with a header saying what it does and what it produces. - Annotate chunks of code rather than every line: what the chunk does, *why*, and **which result in the paper it produces** (e.g. `# Poisson GLM of offspring by strain; results in Table 2`). - Section markers such as `# ---- 1. Load ----` make the script collapsible and easier to navigate. - Code embedded in a Quarto or R Markdown document alongside its explanation counts too. The cleaning script's exclusion comments (*"TO = 9999: undocumented sentinel meaning 'offspring not recorded'… we exclude them and record the count so the loss is visible in the methods section"*) are annotation; `# read the data` next to `read_csv()` is not. ::: All four are needed: perfect comments won't save a hard-coded path, and portable code is no use if nobody knows which file to run first. TADA! also comes before code review, because a reviewer can only check code they can open, run and understand (this afternoon's four Rs, [Ivimey-Cook et al. 2023](https://doi.org/10.1111/jeb.14230)). :::{.callout-tip} **The TADA Wiki.** For practical, step-by-step help with each letter, use the **TADA Wiki**: . It has a *Start here* route to getting your code ready to submit, a chapter for each principle, and guidance on licences, choosing a repository, the SORTEE guidelines and code review, with examples in R and Python. ::: :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} **Exercise: map TADA! onto the cleaning script (5 minutes)** :::: ::::{.task-container} Scroll back to `01_data_cleaning.R`. Identify one specific line or block that demonstrates each of the four TADA! principles. One of them is only *partially* present in the script as it stands — which, and what's missing? Type your answer in Slack. :::: :::
**Available** is the partial one. The script is *written* in a way that could be archived, but on its own a script is not Available: that requires depositing the project in Zenodo or Figshare, with a DOI that the paper cites. We close that gap in Part 5. **Documented** is only partly there too. The header describes the data, but nothing yet records the package versions or a licence. Those belong in the README, which you build next.
### Step 3: Build the README with READMEBuilder A README is the single most useful file in an archive for anyone trying to reuse it, and it is also the file that gets skipped under deadline pressure. Writing one from a blank page is hard; filling in a structured form is not. [**READMEBuilder**](https://github.com/EIvimeyCook/READMEBuilder) provides that form. It turns a project folder into a `README.md`: it summarises every data file column by column, records the script run order, detects package versions and maps the folder. You add what only you know, such as what the columns mean. It runs on your own computer, so nothing is uploaded. :::{.callout-note collapse="true"} ## The six tabs 1. **Project Info:** title, description, abstract, instructions, DOIs, citation, authors (with ORCIDs), affiliations, contact, funders and acknowledgements. Code and data get **separate licences**, with one-click buttons for the usual choices (MIT, Apache 2.0 or GPL-3.0 for code; CC0 or CC BY 4.0 for data). 2. **Files:** load the project folder. The app draws a map of the folder and summarises every data file column by column (type, range, levels, missing values). You add a description of each column, and units for numeric ones. 3. **Script Order:** put the scripts in the order they should be run, with a line on what each one does. 4. **R Packages:** scans your scripts for every package they use and records its version and the R version. If the folder has an `renv.lock`, the versions come from there, and a **Source** column says where each version came from. 5. **Models (optional):** for each analysis, the outcome and predictors, and where the method is described, where the results are reported, and which script and line produce them. 6. **Preview & Export:** a live preview, and a one-click download of `README.md`. Because the structure is fixed, every README it produces covers what TADA!'s *Documented* principle asks for, and you can re-open a README it made earlier and keep editing it. ::: :::{.callout-note} ## Installing and running READMEBuilder READMEBuilder is not on CRAN. Install the development version from GitHub (it has the latest features and fixes; you only need to do this once): ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} install.packages("pak") pak::pak("EIvimeyCook/READMEBuilder@development") packageVersion("READMEBuilder") # 0.2.1 is the development version ``` ::: Then open your project (the RStudio project from Step 1) and start the app with that folder already loaded: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(READMEBuilder) build_readme(here::here()) # open the app on this project build_readme(here::here(), edit_readme = TRUE) # carry on editing a README it made earlier ``` ::: `build_readme()` on its own opens an empty form: then click **Use working directory** on the **Files** tab. The **How to use this app** button at the bottom of the left-hand menu explains each tab. Install `jsonlite` too if you want versions read from an `renv.lock`. ::: :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} **Exercise: build the README (15 minutes)** :::: ::::{.task-container} Run `build_readme(here::here())` from your C. elegans project and work through the tabs. What happens to a row where `TO` is `NA`?
:::{.quiz-explain} **It is dropped.** `NA != 9999` gives `NA`, not `TRUE`, and `filter()` keeps only rows where every condition is `TRUE`. The row disappears without a message and without a line in the exclusion log, so if your data could contain `NA` counts, count and log them explicitly. ::: :::: ::::{.quiz-q} You put your code on GitHub and paste the repository URL into the paper. Which TADA! letter is still not met? :::{.quiz-explain} **Available.** GitHub is for developing code: it gives no DOI, and files can be changed or deleted after publication. Archive a release on Zenodo or Figshare and cite that version's DOI. ::: :::: ::::{.quiz-q} Which comment is annotation in the TADA! sense?
:::{.quiz-explain} Good annotation says what a chunk does, **why**, and which result it produces. `# read the data` only repeats what `read_csv()` already says. ::: :::: ::::{.quiz-q} True or false? You must use `renv` to meet TADA!'s *Transferable* principle. :::{.quiz-explain} **False.** Transferable needs plain code files, relative paths and one project folder archived together. TADA! treats `renv` and containers as helpful extras beyond its minimum. ::: :::: ::::: --- ## Part 5: The SORTEE Guidelines and archiving {#repro-sortee} *⏱ ~15 minutes* TADA! is the floor; the SORTEE guidelines ([Pick et al. 2026](https://doi.org/10.24072/pcjournal.687)) build full quality control on top of it. For every archive: - **Add a licence.** Without one, all rights are reserved, so nobody can legally reuse your work. Typically [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/) for data and [MIT](https://opensource.org/licenses/MIT) (or GPL) for code; they can differ within one archive. Dryad only offers CC0, which doesn't suit code. [choosealicense.com](https://choosealicense.com/) helps. - **Archive with a DOI.** OSF pages and GitHub repositories can be edited or deleted. Link GitHub to Zenodo or Figshare so every release gets its own DOI (Software Heritage works too), and cite the version that produced your results. ### Pre-submission checklist ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Pre-submission checklist: TADA! + SORTEE Guidelines
Done Item
TADA!: Transferable
☐ T: code saved as .R files (not inside Word or PDF)

☐ T: a colleague has run the code on their machine
TADA!: Available
☐ A: code archived in Zenodo or Figshare (or Software Heritage) with a DOI
☐ A: the DOI of the version that produced the results is cited in the paper
TADA!: Documented

☐ D: R version and every package version recorded (README, renv.lock or saved sessionInfo())
☐ D: licence stated for the code (MIT / GPL) and for the data (CC BY / CC0)
TADA!: Annotated
☐ A: each script has a header saying what it does and produces
☐ A: chunk comments say what, why, and which result in the paper each produces
Data (SORTEE)
☐ Raw data preserved unmodified in data/raw/
☐ All exclusion criteria coded and counts saved to exclusion_log.csv
☐ Sentinel values (e.g. 9999) documented in a codebook, not silently dropped
☐ Data archived with a persistent DOI
Code review

Term Definition
Analytical reproducibility Different analysts following the same stated methods reach the same conclusions
Computational reproducibility The same code and data produce identical outputs when run by another person
Many analysts paradigm Multiple independent teams analyse the same dataset to quantify analytical variability
Researcher degrees of freedom The space of defensible analytical decisions in an underspecified analysis (Simmons et al. 2011)
Garden of forking paths The metaphor for multiple valid analytical paths through any dataset (Gelman & Loken 2013)
Sentinel value A special number used to encode meaning, e.g. 9999 standing in for 'not recorded'; must be documented and handled explicitly
TADA! Transferable, Available, Documented, Annotated: the minimum requirements for sharing functional analysis code (Ivimey-Cook et al. 2025, preprint v3)
FAIR Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable — principles for open research data (Wilkinson et al. 2016)
SORTEE Society for Open, Reliable, and Transparent Ecology and Evolutionary Biology
Replication crisis The finding that many published results fail when independently repeated; also called the reproducibility crisis
CC BY 4.0 Creative Commons Attribution — reuse permitted with attribution
MIT Permissive open-source code licence requiring only attribution
